chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In this video we are going to cover Python modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: They allow you to do 3 major things.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Number 1, they can give you some extra functionality via the Python standard library.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example random values, or square root functions, or anything like that.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Besides that, they can also help you to organize your code via multiple files.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: i.e. we have our code spread over multiple Python files,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then we are importing things into one Python file that actually runs the code.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Finally, what is arguably most important, modules allow us to import external modules,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: i.e. modules made by other people than the Python team.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This is where Python really becomes powerful,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: because you can import data analysis modules, game modules, basically anything you want.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I'll cover that at the end.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: First of all though, we can work with the Python standard library.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This is just a set of inbuilt modules that give you lots of commonly used tools.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Like for example the math module for square root, and then sine, cosine and tangent.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: There is also a module for random numbers, and a module for the alphabet.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So if you ever need the strings of the alphabet, it's quite easy to get.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: You don't have to write it by hand.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Back in the code editor, I want to once again create a new file,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and let's call this one modules.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: First of all, to get access to a module, we have to import it via the import statement.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And this usually happens all the way at the top.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: There for example we can find a module like math.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This one gives you access to lots of math functionalities.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Earlier in this series, we for example had the issue that we couldn't get the square root of a number.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The way around that was that, for example to get the square root of 4,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: we simply took the power of one half.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: That way we get 2 as a result.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But doing this kind of operation is not ideal.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And the math module can help you with that, because in there we have a square root function.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: To access that, we have to use the math module like a class, or rather like an instance of a class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: We can simply type a dot, and then we get access to all of the math function it contains.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The one we care about right now is sqrt, short for square root.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In there we want to have one number, in my case a 4.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And now if I run the code, we're getting the same result.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Meaning with that, we have very easy access to a square root.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: On top of that, the math module has a huge amount of stuff that you could work with.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example there's aton, we have a ceiling, we have cosine,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: we have exponential functions, and basically anything you could work with in terms of math.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Besides that, another useful module that I also have to import is called random.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Random gives you, well, random numbers.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The way you would access that is print random,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then once again you get a whole bunch of methods that you could be working with.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: randint is one of the more common ones.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This one you have to call, and we have to specify two integers.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's say we want to get a random number between 0 and 10.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If I now run the code again, we're getting 6, I run it again, 7,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and we always get a random value between 0, and then we go all the way up to 10.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So for randint, the 10 is included.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And well, that is all you have to understand for the basics of importing Python standard modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: All you really need is to do some research to find the modules that are useful for your specific purpose.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For that sort of thing, you want to use Google once again.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: You want to look for Python standard library,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then you get to the Python documentation.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: You get a long list of Python modules that you could be working with.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you look in there, for example, we have the random module.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: That's the one we have just seen.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you click on that, you get a huge amount of information in terms of what you can do with it.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It is quite an extensive module, so you do have to read this for a bit.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Now, most of these modules you are never going to touch.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, I have no idea what netrc file processing is.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Same with plist files. I never used any of these modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Most of the time, you have one specific module that you are going to work with,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and this gives you all you really need.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Once again, this is the kind of thing that comes with practice.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The more you work with Python, and the more research you do,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: the more you are going to come across modules that are really helpful for your specific purpose.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Unfortunately, there is no quick or easy way to learn all of them instantaneously.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I suppose what we could be doing, if I go back to Google,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I want to look for Python module for alphabet.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Or Python library. Library and module are the same thing.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you are doing that, you are getting a couple of answers.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, there we have w3 docs.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And if you look at that, you can import string.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And string has the attribute ascii lowercase.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This would give you the entire alphabet in lowercase letters.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The output is going to be all of this.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This would be one example to figure out a module that could be useful for your purposes.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's try this one.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I want to import the string module.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And after that, I can print string and then .ascii lowercase.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Make sure to not call this one.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It is an attribute, not a method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And now if I run all of this, we are getting the entirety of the alphabet.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Both in lowercase and then in uppercase letters.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I should have specified here, I want to have the ascii lowercase.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Now if I run this, we are only getting the lowercase letters.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So all of this is still fairly simple.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Now there is one thing that you can also do.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's say in your particular code, you only need ascii lowercase.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: You don't need anything else from this module or library.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you want to do that, you can change the import setting to something like from string,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I want to import one specific thing.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which is going to be ascii, not letters, but lowercase.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you are doing that, you have ascii lowercase available like any other variable inside of your

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: code.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Meaning I can get rid of the string dot, run the code again,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and we once again get the same output.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It isn't going to be a major difference, but this may be easier to read, at least on occasion.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This would also work with methods.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, if we only care about randint, I wouldn't want to import all of random,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I would from random import randint.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And with that, I don't have a random available anymore.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So if we are calling it like this, we would get an error.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: All we need is randint with the usual arguments.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So if I run this again, we are once again getting a random number.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And with that, we have covered the first part of modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Next up, we can use modules to have larger python projects that work over multiple files.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Basically all we are going to do, is we are going to write python logic over multiple files,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then import things into one particular file, and then run only that file.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For that, back in the code, I want to create a completely new folder, just to keep things

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: organized.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So, new folder, and let's call this one,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: multiple file project.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Not the best name, but it's gonna work for now.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In there, I want to create two python files.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: One is going to be main.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And besides that, let's call it support.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Both of these python files should be inside of the same folder.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And also let me close all of the other files, that way it's a bit easier to follow along.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: We have main.py, and we have support.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I want to get started inside of support.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In there, I can for example create a function.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's call this one, addToNumbers, with number a and number b.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The return value of all of this is simply going to be the sum of numA and numB.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Also, we can create a whole class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's call this one, test.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Could also inherit, but it doesn't really matter.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: What I want to work on is that we have a variable, or rather an attribute a,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: that can get a value of 1, 2, 3.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And then a method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So define.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I suppose we can call this, sum method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: That as always needs self as a parameter.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And in there, we simply want to print sum method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: With that, we have a function, and we have a class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: On top of that, I want to create a simple variable.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The name could be var, and the value does not matter.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Just something is fine.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: All three of these things I want to use inside of main.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And that I can do in a couple of ways.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Most importantly, we will need the import statement.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And then we have to import from the file name.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In our case, this is going to be support.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Because the python file we import is called support.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And support gives us that.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: After I have that, I can use the content of this python file,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: like I would have it available inside of main.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, what I could be doing is simply run test,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then assign it the instance of the class test.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I would need support, and then test.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Don't forget to call this one, and if I run the code now,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: we are not getting an error.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Also, if you look on the left side,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Python has created a pycache folder,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: which you can ignore entirely,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: but it's kind of interesting that it does exist.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It's there to store the connection between these two files.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: All that we want to do is to print test.a,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and we can call test.someMethod,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then we can run all of this,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and we get 1, 2, 3, and some method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Exactly what we have specified inside of the class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: On top of that, we could also print the variable we have created.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: I call this one var.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Although you would have to make sure that you are calling this support.var.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If I now run the code, we are getting something.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The value we once again specified earlier.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Finally, we can get access to the function via support.addToNumbers.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And the numbers I want to add together are 2 and 3.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The result we have to print.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So let me wrap all of this with a print function,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and now we're getting 5.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: All of this is still working just fine.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: On top of that, what you can do,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: if you only need one specific thing from a Python file,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: you can get rid of the import statement,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and replace it with from support, import,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then whatever specific thing you need.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, if I only care about test,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: then I would get the test class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And for that to work, I would have to comment out the other two parts,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: because those wouldn't work anymore.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Simply because we haven't imported them.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Also, it's not support.test anymore,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: it is simply going to be test.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But if I run the code now,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: we are getting 1 to 3 and some method.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The content of the test class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Those two things.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: On top of that, if you want to import multiple things,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: you can import test, then a comma separation, then var,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then addToNumbers.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Python is totally happy to mix the data types,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: so we have a class, a variable, and a function.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Once we have that, I can uncomment things,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and get rid of support.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And now, you can use the variables and the functions,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: literally like anything else inside of this document.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And especially when you have more complex projects,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: this kind of setup is incredibly valuable.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Because you can keep the main logic inside of one file,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then all of the additional stuff inside of another file.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: You never really want to have python files that get too long.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It's simply becoming messy to work with.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But once again, this is the kind of thing that you learn with practice.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For now, I suppose, don't worry too much about it.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Although there's one more thing.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: At the moment, we are importing literally everything from the support.py file.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which we can replace with an asterisk.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: That way, you are importing all of the individual parts of this python file.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which is a bit easier to write.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If I run the code now, we are getting the exact same result.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And the only difference from simply importing the entire support module,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: is that you don't have to write support.py before the class,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: or the variable, or the function you have imported.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It makes it a bit easier to work with.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But that's about it.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which way is better is entirely subjective.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Sometimes you do want to be clear about where a class is coming from.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But other times you don't really care that much,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and you simply want to have the class.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Once again, the difference isn't that important,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: so don't worry too much about it.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But anyway, this is all you need to work over multiple files.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It's fairly straightforward.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which means, next up, we can work on external modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And those are modules made by people who are not part of the python team.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: This is the part where python becomes actually incredibly powerful.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Because external modules can do a lot in python.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, we have pygame, if you want to make games.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: We have map.lib, if you want to make graphs.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And we have something like beautiful soup, if you want to do web scraping.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In case you don't know what that means,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: web scraping means that python can read a website,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then get information or do some kind of interaction with a website.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: There are actually a huge amount of modules that you can import.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Since python is so popular, you have modules for pretty much any kind of purpose.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: The one limitation though that you should be aware of,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: is that you always have to install these modules,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: either via the powershell for windows, or the terminal on macOS.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, in my case, I am going to work on the windows powershell.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you are on macOS, this should be the terminal.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And to install a module, you want to have pip, then install,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and then the name of the module.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For example, in my case, I want to install matplotlib, a graphing library.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: We're going to play around with that in just a second.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Now before you run this, and you are on macOS, this should be pip3, install matplotlib.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But other than that, you are doing the exact same thing.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: In my case, I only want to type pip, and now if I press enter,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: python is going to install this module, and this might take a second.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Also, you have to be connected to the internet to make all of this work.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And after a while, you get everything is installed,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and very often you get that a new release of pip is available.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which you can install with python.exe-m pip install upgrade-pip.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Although I am not going to do that, but keep your pip updated, it's generally good practice.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Anyway, with that, we have one external module.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you want to have another kind of module, or you have some kind of specific purpose in mind,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: this is going to be a research project for you.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: It would take way too long to cover even most of the external python modules.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But anyway, let's create a basic graph.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For that, we are back in the code editor, and I want to create a new python file.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Let's call this one graph.py.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Then I can go into fullscreen.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And first of all, we have to import the module.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Since we have in the powershell the terminal installed matplotlib,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: this is what we also want to import.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So import matplotlib.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Now I want to run the code.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And nothing is going to happen.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And that's a good thing.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: If you are getting an error at this point, something with the install went wrong.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: So double check that.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: But for matplotlib, you don't actually import the entirety of the library,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: because it is quite large.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Instead, you import one specific part of it.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which is going to be matplotlib.pyplot.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Which basically means we are importing the entire library,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: and from that we are taking one specific subpart.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: Also, what I forgot to mention is,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: in the code, writing all of this would be kind of tedious,

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: because there are way too many characters.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: For that, python has a neat keyword called s.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: We want to import this part under another name.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: And for pyplot, this is usually abbreviated as plt.

chunks.title: Modules
chunks.text: That way it's much less typing.

chunks.title: Modules
